ai-governance/dg-01.title: [數據治理 #1] Gen AI 如何提昇金融業的數據治理?
ai-governance/dg-01.content:
這篇文章的影片版（約 1 分鐘，英語旁白、中文字幕）

長期以來數據治理對金融機構來說重要性不言可喻，但往往投入數據治理資源的優先序相對並不高。然而近幾年隨著資料科學、AI乃至於生成式AI（Gen AI）的興起，數據治理的重要性不斷因為技術的演進而進一步「被迫地」突顯出來。在本系列文章將以數據治理 Data Governance 為核心進行不同面向的介紹與探討。
本篇文章將探討 Gen AI 如何提昇金融業的數據治理。
—

依據我們過去豐富的數據治理專案經驗，在八大數據治理的支柱中最普遍的問題不外乎數據品質、數血緣與數據字典這三個彼此之間也有高度相關性的議題。如今Gen AI不僅能提升數據的質量和一致性，還能通過自動化的數據質量檢查和清理流程，確保數據的準確性和可靠性；它還提高了數據管理框架內的透明度和問責度 (Accountability)，使金融機構能夠更有效地追踪和管理數據來源，從而支持更加精確的決策和業務增長。

以下是 Gen AI 可以提昇數據治理的三個基本面向：


元數據(或稱詮釋資料)的建立與補強

依據我們的經驗，元數據 (Metadata) 的缺乏與不夠精確幾乎是造成資料品質不足最普遍的原因，而填寫過程繁瑣常需大量的人工且無一致性的填寫標準是最大的障礙；Gen AI恰恰可提供協助。
舉例而言，本土銀行在系統建置的過程中均有撰寫「商業分析文件 (BA 文件)」以及「系統分析文件(SA 文件)」；而這兩份文件多半可提供相當程度的元數據的資訊基礎。透過 Gen AI自動讀取該些文件而快速生成元數據，已可提高使用者對於資料的可理解性而減少誤用或錯用。
而針對過去舊有資料的元數據補遺而言，Gen AI可讀取既有大量的文件來填補過去系統建置過程中所缺乏的元數據也是可行的做法。


數據品質的監測、比對與清理

於系統運作時及時檢測數據中的異常、錯誤和不一致性是在日常運作中提昇數據治理的務實做法；我們可以透過Gen AI掃描大量數據集識別出缺失值、格式錯誤和數據異常，並及時告警並進行後續的處理。
此外依據我們的經驗，常見存在於不同的資料表單但具有相同的資料名稱的數據彼此之間並不一致。發生此情況的原因存在著多數的可能性，透過 Gen AI 並給予適當的指令可協助數據治理團隊成員辨識原因。


建立數據的知識圖譜

知識圖譜的範圍可能很廣泛，但光就數據血緣 (Lineage) 的不足就是常見的痛點。利用Gen AI透過組織內各種可能包含數據血緣的文件、檔案、系統設定檔甚至是程式碼自動提取數據與數據之間的關聯構建出知識圖譜的基礎，亦為 Gen AI 可提昇數據治理的場景之一。
以上針對 Gen AI 可以提昇數據治理的幾個基本面向進行說明，如果您針對數據治理有更多更深入的需求，歡迎與我們聯繫。我們在台灣、香港、新加坡有著豐富協助金融業處理數據治理的經驗。

ai-governance/dg-02.title: [數據治理 #2] 數據治理常見的迷思
ai-governance/dg-02.content:
這篇文章的影片版（約 1 分鐘，英語旁白、中文字幕）

💡 [數據治理 #2] 數據治理常見的迷思
💡[Data Governance #2] Common Misconceptions About Data Governance
長期以來數據治理對金融機構來說重要性不言可喻，但往往投入數據治理資源的優先序相對並不高。然而近幾年隨著資料科學、AI乃至於生成式AI（Gen AI）的興起，數據治理的重要性不斷因為技術的演進而進一步「被迫地」突顯出來。在本系列文章將以數據治理 Data Governance 為核心進行不同面向的介紹與探討。
本篇文章將介紹：數據治理常見的迷思。

我們曾與多個金融領域的客戶進行有關數據治理的訪談，在訪談中我們常常向客戶詢問他們所理解的數據治理為何，如何進行，以及該由誰負責等與日常業務中高度相關的問題。然而從我們所蒐集的回復中常常發現值得進一步研議的問題甚至是迷思。
以下是我們從最常見的迷思中所挑出的三項。

1️⃣採購資料倉儲軟體就可順利完成數據治理:在我們實際訪談金融業的經驗中，不時聽到一個問題：「明明已經採購了資料倉儲軟體與相關系統，數據仍然有很多問題」。顯然有相當多的組織仍存在著要解決數據治理就是先採購系統的觀念，以及採用了系統就像吃了萬靈丹一樣可以高枕無憂。

2️⃣數據治理是 IT 的事，與業務&其他單位無關:由於絕大多數的數據都是儲存於資料庫中，而資料庫系統大多由 IT 單位管理或作為負責單位或 Owner；所以數據治理當然就是 IT 單位應該要負責的事情。

3️⃣ 數據治理僅為短期的專案，不需持續執行:在眾多訪談的經驗中，我們常被問到數據治理是否能在某一段期間內「完成」？顯見企業並沒有將數據治理如同風險管理一樣看待；數據治理其實是一項需要長期運作的事項。 以上三項是我們在過去的專案與訪談中相當普遍的迷思，也多半是導致客戶在執行數據治理時產生障礙的主因；我們會在後續的文章中進一步解釋並調整這些迷思。

您好，我是星普思 Synpulse Taiwan 的副合夥人 David。星普思為發跡於瑞士且專精於金融業已逾 25年的外商管理顧問公司；我們透過提供管理顧問服務，並運用領先的科技與數位技術來協助客戶解決問題或達成營運目標。
若您有數位轉型、AI轉型、風險管理與永續發展ESG等相關的議題，歡迎洽詢。

ai-governance/dg-03.title: [數據治理 #3] 數據治理常見的痛點
ai-governance/dg-03.content:
這篇文章的影片版（約 1 分鐘，英語旁白、中文字幕）

長期以來數據治理對金融機構來說重要性不言可喻，但往往投入數據治理資源的優先序相對並不高。然而近幾年隨著資料科學、AI乃至於生成式AI（Gen AI）的興起，數據治理的重要性不斷因為技術的演進而進一步「被迫地」突顯出來。在本系列文章將以數據治理 Data Governance 為核心進行不同面向的介紹與探討。
本篇文章將介紹：數據治理常見的痛點。

我們曾與多個金融領域的客戶進行有關數據治理的訪談，在訪談中我們最重要的問題即為常遇到的痛點有哪些？
以下是我們整理出最常見的三項痛點。

1️⃣ 數據品質不佳
數據品質不佳幾乎是一個大家共通的問題，至少我們鮮少聽到有客戶認為自己的品質是足夠良好的。而數據品質不佳的狀況也有很多種，形成的原因也有多種可能性。一般而言不外乎：數據的數值或資訊不正確或不夠精確，以及在數據進行整併的時候(多半在系統整合時發生)發現理應是相同的數據但卻有不同的數值…等。然而更令人氣餒的是，當要進行問題的追查時，卻發現數據的上下游關係，亦即俗稱的「血緣」並不完整而導致追查不易。

2️⃣ 數據治理的權責不明
在我們的經驗中，設有數據治理團隊的組織已相對不常見，有明確的角色與責任(R&R)的組織更是少之又少。而在權責定義不清楚的情況下，人員在執行相關的任務時即會產生困擾，導致執行的優先順序錯亂進而使得整體數據治理的成效不彰。更明白地說，若是無明確的績效定義，組織要推動數據治理將是難上加難。

3️⃣ 無法評估未來應導入的系統工具
一般而言組織已經為了業務應用所產生的數據已經採購了相當數量的系統工具；即便如此我們仍然常常聽到客戶抱怨所採購的工具並不適用或是無法滿足需求，然而更糟糕的是，後續應該進一步導入的系統工具為何，以及優先順序甚至無法評估。

以上是我們最常於金融機構聽到的數據治理的痛點，後續我們會再持續討論相關痛點的發生原因，以及可行的解決方案。

ai-governance/dg-04.title: [數據治理 #4] 資料策略
ai-governance/dg-04.content:
這篇文章的影片版（約 1 分鐘，英語旁白、中文字幕）

💡[數據治理 #4] 資料策略
💡[Data Governance #4] Data Strategy
長期以來數據治理對金融機構來說重要性不言可喻，但往往投入數據治理資源的優先序相對並不高。然而近幾年隨著資料科學、AI乃至於生成式AI（Gen AI）的興起，數據治理的重要性不斷因為技術的演進而進一步「被迫地」突顯出來。在本系列文章將以數據治理 Data Governance 為核心進行不同面向的介紹與探討。

本篇文章將介紹：數據治理中的資料策略。
資料策略不僅僅是一份處理資料的發展藍圖，且是一個組織面對資料時的願景，並且將資料管理的實務與您的業務目標對標。沒有資料策略，資料治理可能會淪為僵化的合規活動，與組織目標脫節導致看不出實際的成效。
定義資料策略為何對於數據治理如此重要？

1️⃣ 才能有明確的目標：數據治理常見的議題之一是不知為何而戰，透過定義明確的資料策略的過程，組織內部將取得一致的戰略性目標。
2️⃣才知道執行哪些決策：有了目標之後，即能進一步依據目標而產生出行動方案；而在行動方案執行的過程中亦將明確知悉資料將被用於進行哪些決策。
3️⃣才能有效運用資源：在組織的人力、時間、預算有限的情況下，有了資料策略即能正確地判斷資源應當投入於哪些層面而減少衝突、重工與浪費。

總的來說，數據治理往往讓人垢病的議題之一即為投入了大量的資源卻不見明確的成果；缺乏明確的資料策略可能是主因。有了資料策略，能協助您的數據治理的成效更為有感，更能讓數據為您的組織帶來更大的價值。

ai-governance/dg-05.title: [數據治理 #5] 黃金規則
ai-governance/dg-05.content:
這篇文章的影片版（約 1 分鐘，英語旁白、中文字幕）

💡[數據治理 #5] 黃金規則
💡[Data Governance #5] Golden Rules
長期以來數據治理對金融機構來說重要性不言可喻，但往往投入數據治理資源的優先序相對並不高。然而近幾年隨著資料科學、AI乃至於生成式AI（Gen AI）的興起，數據治理的重要性不斷因為技術的演進而進一步「被迫地」突顯出來。在本系列文章將以數據治理 Data Governance 為核心進行不同面向的介紹與探討。

本篇文章將介紹：數據治理中的黃金規則。
數據治理中的黃金規則，最重要的角色就是確保數據品質符合要求，對於提升組織的運營效率、降低合規風險以及構建組織對於數據的信任基礎非常重要。

以下介紹常見的幾種黃金規則：
1️⃣ 標準化規則：確認數據滿足事先定義好的數據標準
2️⃣ 驗證規則：驗證數據的值域、格式或型態符合需求；例如年齡不能為負值
3️⃣ 去重複規則：決定多筆相似的數據該如何合併
4️⃣ 補遺規則：當數據發生缺漏時進行補遺時的規則
5️⃣ 一致性與參考完整性規則：確定數據符合業務邏輯性；例如合約終止日期不得早於開始日期
6️⃣ 優先權規則：數據發生不一致時，需決定優先使用哪一項數據

除了上述常見的6項規則之外，實務中仍尚有其他黃金規則。一般而言，組織將視實際數據所發生的狀況依據數據的重要性或優先序逐一進行黃金規則的討論。此外，黃金規則的設計亦與業務作業習慣有關，未來落地時也可能需要調整作業流程。
總的來說，黃金規則最後能夠完整落地，除了規則本身之外尚有「系統」與「作業流程」需要一併配合。

ai-governance/dg-06.title: [數據治理 #6] 數據治理如何落地?
ai-governance/dg-06.content:
這篇文章的影片版（約 1 分鐘，英語旁白、中文字幕）

近期接到多個客戶以及合作夥伴的提問，關於數據治理總是無法落地的問題。在本篇文章中將重點式地介紹我們的經驗與觀察，並且提供發想的方向供參考。
Data Governance 為何無法落地？——從框架到真正產生價值
在當今企業數位化轉型的浪潮中，Data Governance（數據治理）成為了許多企業的關鍵策略之一。然而，許多企業投入大量資源，導入了各類框架、標準與系統，卻仍然難以真正落地，無法在業務中創造實際價值。這種「有框架、無應用」的現象，究竟是什麼原因造成的？又該如何避免？

許多企業在數據治理的推動上，往往會遇到以下幾種常見的「未落地」情境：
1️⃣ 導入了框架，卻難以套用
許多企業從顧問或業界標準中導入了 Data Governance 框架，但這些框架可能過於理論化，與企業的實際業務場景脫節，導致難以真正應用。
2️⃣ 建立了數據標準，卻未被依循
許多企業雖然設立了數據標準，但卻沒有相應的機制來確保這些標準被遵循。例如，數據格式標準雖然制定了，但不同部門仍各自為政，導致數據品質依舊參差不齊。
3️⃣ 採購了大型系統，但無法滿足需求
許多企業認為購買一個強大的數據管理系統，就能解決數據治理問題。然而，若缺乏清晰的需求分析與內部使用者的參與，這些系統最終可能無法真正解決業務痛點。
4️⃣ 建立了管理流程，但仍存在漏洞
一些企業花費大量時間建立數據治理的管理流程，但缺乏強制執行與監督機制，導致實際執行時依然出現數據錯誤、流程不透明等問題。
這些現象的本質問題在於：企業到底是買了一個「精美的系統」，還是讓數據治理真正成為業務運營的一部分？

為什麼 Data Governance 會難以落地？
那麼，為何這些數據治理計畫無法真正落地？根本原因可以歸納為以下幾點：
🔍 1. 顧問提供的框架是否千篇一律？
許多企業依賴顧問公司提供的標準化框架，但這些框架往往是通用模板，缺乏針對企業自身業務模式與數據需求的客製化調整。當這些框架無法貼合企業實際運營時，自然難以落地。
🔍 2. 理想規劃與實際執行的落差是否被考量？
許多數據治理計畫在規劃階段看似完美，但在落地執行時，卻因組織文化、技術限制或人員意識等因素，導致無法真正推動。企業往往高估了員工對新標準與流程的接受度，而忽略了變革管理的重要性。
🔍 3. 技術主導 vs. 業務主導：誰應該負責？
很多數據治理專案由 IT 部門主導，但 IT 與業務部門的目標往往不同。IT 部門關注技術架構與系統落實，而業務部門則希望能快速應用數據解決實際問題。若企業未能在技術與業務之間找到平衡，數據治理便難以真正產生價值。
說到底，數據治理在 「治什麼」？ 和 「理什麼」？您的組織是否真的瞭解並且「在同一頁上 (On the same page)」？
換句話說，企業應該先釐清自己希望解決的數據痛點，才能制定合適的治理策略，而不是盲目導入框架與系統。

而如何真正讓 Data Governance 落地？
在推動數據治理落地之前，企業應該先自問以下幾個問題：
💡 1. 我們缺少的是方法論與框架嗎？
若企業對數據治理的概念仍不清晰，可以先引入合適的方法論與框架，但更重要的是確保這些框架能與企業的業務需求相結合，而非僅僅參考業界標準。
💡 2. 我們缺少的是一個強而有力的知名系統嗎？
一個好的數據治理系統確實能夠提升管理效率，但它不應該是解決問題的唯一手段。企業應該先確保數據治理的規則與流程被明確定義，再選擇合適的技術工具來支撐這些規則。
💡 3. 我們缺少的是各式各樣的流程嗎？
有些企業認為建立了完整的流程就能解決數據治理問題，但若缺乏有效的執行與監督，這些流程可能只是紙上談兵。企業應該確保治理流程能夠真正與日常業務運營相結合，而不是獨立於業務之外。
我們都會建議客戶：就算上面的問題都解決了，是否就可以落地了？如果不行，那落地的障礙在哪裡？
結語：「落地」才能「產生價值」；精美的投影片與華麗的系統沒有辦法。

ai-governance/dg-07.title: [數據治理 #7] 從 CDO，到CAO，再到 “CDAIO”，會不會又是一種 ”頭銜通膨”?
ai-governance/dg-07.content:
這篇文章的影片版（約 1 分鐘，英語旁白、中文字幕）

近期 HBR 發表了一篇文章《Why Your Company Needs a Chief Data, Analytics, and AI Officer》
lnkd.in/gdcuG7Gz
探討了 CDAIO 這個頭銜。
這些年來，組織內關於資料主管 ( Data leader ) 這個角色 C-Suite 的頭銜不斷演進：從 CDO (Chief Data Officer)、CDAO (Chief Data and Analytics Officer)，演變至今日的 CDAIO (Chief Data, Analytics, and AI Officer)。
坦白說，客戶面對這樣的C-Suite頭銜議題時總是半信半疑。許多人一定在想，這該不會只是一種頭銜通膨（Title Inflation）？」但是，我也常會問客戶的問題是：「如果 AI 無法發揮價值，現在誰會被挑戰/問責？」
當我們與客戶討論這樣的議題時，最終都還是會回歸到很務實的核心議題：這個角色的責任到底是什麼？以我的觀察，這是金融業在數位浪潮下，這三個頭銜的演化代表了金融業看待資料的三種截然不同之戰略思維轉變。
以下簡單總結了三個時期各自最關注的核心任務、痛點以及三個關鍵議題：
1️⃣ CDO 時期：奠基與防守
🟥 主要痛點： 我們有海量數據，但沒人敢用，因為沒人知道哪個數字是對的。
🟪 核心任務： 建立「單一真理版本 (Single Source of Truth)」。
🟦 關鍵挑戰： 這是一個辛苦的基礎工程——確保資料品質、滿足監管合規 (Compliance)、打破部門穀倉 (Silos)。這時期的數據被視為一種「資產」，需要被嚴格保護與盤點。
2️⃣ CDAO 時期：從成本中心轉向價值中心
🟥主要痛點： 數據整理好了，但董事會開始問：「我們花了幾千萬建 Data Lake，買了Data Warehouse，ROI 在哪裡？」
🟪核心任務： 數據民主化與商業變現。
🟦關鍵挑戰： 不再只是「儲存資料」，而是「分析」。如何讓數據走出 IT 部門，賦能前線業務（Data Democratization），並透過進階分析（Advanced Analytics）主動出擊，從防守轉向進攻得分。
3️⃣ CDAIO 時期：AI 的規模化與融合
🟥主要痛點： 每個人都在談 GenAI，POC跟沙盒做了一堆，但真正能落地進入核心業務場景的有多少呢？
🟪核心任務： 駕馭「三位一體」的複雜性——Data 是燃料，Analytics 是引擎，AI 是領航。
🟦關鍵挑戰：AI 治理與風險、從實驗室走到營運各方面的鴻溝、「三位一體」下的組織架構與責任調整是否有對應的調整？
總結來說，如果今天董事會提問：『資料與 AI 到底替我們賺了多少錢、降了多少風險？』，在場的每個人是否有相同的答案呢？

en/ai-governance/dg-01.title: [Data Governance #1] How Can GenAI Strengthen Data Governance in Financial Services?
en/ai-governance/dg-01.content:
Video version of this article (about 1 minute, English narration)

Financial institutions have long accepted that data governance matters, yet it rarely comes first when resources are allocated. Over the past few years, the rise of data science, AI and now generative AI (GenAI) has changed that: each step forward in the technology has forced data governance further into the spotlight. This series looks at data governance from several angles.
This first article asks how GenAI can strengthen data governance in financial services.
—

Across our data governance projects, the most common problems among the eight pillars of data governance are data quality, data lineage and the data dictionary, three issues that are closely linked to one another. GenAI can do more than lift the quality and consistency of data: through automated quality checks and cleansing, it helps keep data accurate and reliable. It also brings more transparency and accountability to the data management framework, so institutions can trace and manage their data sources more effectively, which supports sharper decisions and business growth.

Here are three basic ways GenAI can strengthen data governance:


Creating and enriching metadata

In our experience, missing or imprecise metadata is the most common root cause of poor data quality. The biggest obstacle is the filling-in itself: it is tedious, labour-intensive and done without a consistent standard. This is exactly where GenAI can help.
For example, when banks in Taiwan build a system, they produce a business analysis document (BA document) and a system analysis document (SA document). Between them, these two documents usually hold much of the information that metadata needs. Having GenAI read them and generate metadata automatically already makes data easier to understand and reduces the risk of it being misused.
For legacy data, GenAI can also read the large body of existing documentation to fill in metadata that was never captured when older systems were built.


Monitoring, reconciling and cleansing data quality

Catching anomalies, errors and inconsistencies while systems are running is a practical way to strengthen data governance day to day. GenAI can scan large datasets to identify missing values, format errors and outliers, then raise timely alerts so they can be dealt with.
We also often find that fields with the same name in different tables do not agree with each other. There can be many reasons for this; given the right prompts, GenAI can help the data governance team work out which one applies.


Building a knowledge graph of data

A knowledge graph can cover a lot of ground, but missing data lineage alone is a common pain point. GenAI can extract the relationships between data elements from documents, files, system configuration files and even source code that may hold lineage information, and use them to lay the foundation of a knowledge graph. This is another way GenAI can strengthen data governance.
These are some of the basic ways GenAI can strengthen data governance. If you would like to go further, please get in touch. We have extensive experience helping financial institutions with data governance in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore.

en/ai-governance/dg-02.title: [Data Governance #2] Common Misconceptions About Data Governance
en/ai-governance/dg-02.content:

💡 [Data Governance #2] Common Misconceptions About Data Governance
Financial institutions have long accepted that data governance matters, yet it rarely comes first when resources are allocated. Over the past few years, the rise of data science, AI and now generative AI (GenAI) has changed that: each step forward in the technology has forced data governance further into the spotlight. This series looks at data governance from several angles.
This article looks at common misconceptions about data governance.

We have interviewed many clients in financial services about data governance. In these interviews we often ask questions that are closely tied to their day-to-day business: what they understand data governance to be, how it should be done, and who should be responsible for it. The answers often point to issues worth a closer look, and sometimes to outright misconceptions.
Here are three of the most common misconceptions we have picked out.

1️⃣ Buying data warehouse software is enough to get data governance done: In our interviews across the financial industry, we regularly hear the same question: “We have already bought data warehouse software and the related systems, so why does our data still have so many problems?” Clearly, many organisations still believe that solving data governance starts with buying a system, and that once the system is in place, it works like a cure-all and they can rest easy.

2️⃣ Data governance is IT’s job and has nothing to do with the business or other units: Most data is stored in databases, and database systems are mostly managed or owned by the IT unit. So data governance must surely be IT’s responsibility.

3️⃣ Data governance is a short-term project, not an ongoing effort: In many interviews, we are often asked whether data governance can be “completed” within a set period. This shows that companies do not treat data governance the way they treat risk management; in fact, data governance needs to run over the long term. These three misconceptions came up again and again in our past projects and interviews, and they are often the main reason clients run into obstacles when they put data governance into practice. In later articles we will explain them further and show how to correct them.

en/ai-governance/dg-03.title: [Data Governance #3] Common Pain Points in Data Governance
en/ai-governance/dg-03.content:
Video version of this article (about 1 minute, English narration)

Financial institutions have long accepted that data governance matters, yet it rarely comes first when resources are allocated. Over the past few years, the rise of data science, AI and now generative AI (GenAI) has changed that: each step forward in the technology has forced data governance further into the spotlight. This series looks at data governance from several angles.
This article looks at common pain points in data governance.

We have interviewed many clients in financial services about data governance, and the most important question we ask is: which pain points do you run into most often?
Here are the three most common pain points we have identified.

1️⃣ Poor data quality
Poor data quality is a problem almost everyone shares; we rarely hear a client say their data quality is good enough. It takes many forms and can have many causes. Typically, values or information are incorrect or not precise enough, or, when data is consolidated (usually during system integration), data that should be identical turns out to have different values. More discouraging still, when you try to trace the problem, you find that the upstream and downstream relationships of the data, commonly known as data lineage, are incomplete, which makes tracing difficult.

2️⃣ Unclear roles and responsibilities for data governance
In our experience, organisations with a data governance team are relatively uncommon, and those with clearly defined roles and responsibilities (R&R) are rarer still. When accountability is unclear, people struggle to carry out the related tasks, priorities get muddled, and data governance as a whole delivers little. To put it plainly, without clear definitions of performance, driving data governance across an organisation is an uphill battle.

3️⃣ No way to assess which system tools to adopt next
Organisations have usually already bought a good number of system tools for the data their business generates. Even so, we often hear clients complain that the tools they bought do not fit or cannot meet their needs. Worse still, they cannot even assess which system tools to adopt next, or in what order.

These are the data governance pain points we hear most often at financial institutions. In later articles we will look at why they arise and at possible solutions.

en/ai-governance/dg-04.title: [Data Governance #4] Data Strategy
en/ai-governance/dg-04.content:
Video version of this article (about 1 minute, English narration)

💡[Data Governance #4] Data Strategy
Financial institutions have long accepted that data governance matters, yet it rarely comes first when resources are allocated. Over the past few years, the rise of data science, AI and now generative AI (GenAI) has changed that: each step forward in the technology has forced data governance further into the spotlight. This series looks at data governance from several angles.

This article looks at data strategy within data governance.
A data strategy is more than a roadmap for handling data. It sets out an organisation’s vision for its data and aligns data management practice with your business goals. Without a data strategy, data governance can turn into a rigid compliance exercise, cut off from the organisation’s goals and with no visible results.
Why does defining a data strategy matter so much for data governance?

1️⃣ Clear goals: a common problem in data governance is not knowing what you are fighting for. Defining a clear data strategy brings the whole organisation onto the same strategic goals.
2️⃣ Knowing which decisions the data serves: once the goals are set, they can be turned into action plans. As those plans are carried out, it also becomes clear which decisions the data will be used to make.
3️⃣ Using resources effectively: people, time and budget are always limited. With a data strategy, an organisation can judge correctly where to put its resources, with less conflict, rework and waste.

Overall, one of the most common criticisms of data governance is that it consumes a lot of resources without producing clear results, and the lack of a clear data strategy may well be the main reason. A data strategy makes the results of your data governance more tangible and helps your data bring more value to your organisation.

en/ai-governance/dg-05.title: [Data Governance #5] Golden Rules
en/ai-governance/dg-05.content:
Video version of this article (about 1 minute, English narration)

💡[Data Governance #5] Golden Rules
Financial institutions have long accepted that data governance matters, yet it rarely comes first when resources are allocated. Over the past few years, the rise of data science, AI and now generative AI (GenAI) has changed that: each step forward in the technology has forced data governance further into the spotlight. This series looks at data governance from several angles.

This article looks at golden rules in data governance.
The main job of golden rules in data governance is to make sure data quality meets requirements. They matter a great deal for running the organisation more efficiently, reducing compliance risk and building the organisation’s trust in its data.

Here are some common golden rules:
1️⃣ Standardisation rules: check that data meets predefined data standards
2️⃣ Validation rules: check that the range, format or type of data values meets requirements; for example, age cannot be negative
3️⃣ De-duplication rules: decide how several similar records should be merged
4️⃣ Gap-filling rules: rules for filling in data that is missing
5️⃣ Consistency and referential integrity rules: make sure data follows business logic; for example, a contract’s end date cannot be earlier than its start date
6️⃣ Priority rules: when data is inconsistent, decide which value takes precedence

Beyond these six common rules, there are other golden rules in practice. Organisations usually work through golden rules one by one, based on the problems they actually see in their data and on how important or urgent each data item is. The design of golden rules also depends on how the business operates day to day, so operating processes may need to change when the rules are put in place.
In short, putting golden rules fully in place takes more than the rules themselves: the systems and the operating processes have to support them too.

en/ai-governance/dg-06.title: [Data Governance #6] How Can Data Governance Be Put into Practice?
en/ai-governance/dg-06.content:
Video version of this article (about 1 minute, English narration)

Recently, several clients and partners have asked us the same question: why does data governance never seem to be put into practice? This article highlights our experience and observations, and offers some directions to think about.
Why does data governance fail to take hold? From framework to real value
In today’s wave of digital transformation, data governance has become a key strategy for many organisations. Yet many of them invest heavily, bringing in frameworks, standards and systems of every kind, and still struggle to put it into practice or to create real value for the business. What causes this pattern of “frameworks without application”, and how can it be avoided?

When driving data governance forward, many organisations run into the same few situations in which it is never put into practice:
1️⃣ A framework was introduced, but it is hard to apply
Many organisations bring in a data governance framework from consultants or industry standards. But these frameworks can be too theoretical and detached from the organisation’s actual business scenarios, so they are hard to apply in reality.
2️⃣ Data standards were set, but they are not followed
Many organisations set data standards but have no mechanism to make sure they are followed. For example, a data format standard has been defined, yet each department still goes its own way, so data quality remains uneven.
3️⃣ A large system was bought, but it does not meet the need
Many organisations believe that buying a powerful data management system will solve their data governance problems. Without a clear needs analysis and the involvement of internal users, however, these systems may end up not solving the real business pain points.
4️⃣ Management processes were built, but gaps remain
Some organisations spend a great deal of time building data governance processes but lack enforcement and oversight, so data errors and opaque processes still appear when the work is actually carried out.
The underlying question behind all of this is: did the organisation buy a “polished system”, or has data governance truly become part of how the business runs?

Why is data governance so hard to put into practice?
So why do these data governance programmes fail to take hold? The root causes come down to the following:
🔍 1. Are the consultants’ frameworks one-size-fits-all?
Many organisations rely on standardised frameworks from consulting firms. These are often generic templates, not tailored to the organisation’s own business model and data needs. When a framework does not fit how the organisation actually operates, it is naturally hard to put into practice.
🔍 2. Has the gap between the ideal plan and actual execution been considered?
Many data governance programmes look perfect at the planning stage, but stall during execution because of organisational culture, technical constraints or staff awareness. Organisations often overestimate how readily employees will accept new standards and processes, and overlook the importance of change management.
🔍 3. Technology-led vs business-led: who should own it?
Many data governance projects are led by IT, but IT and the business often have different goals. IT focuses on technical architecture and system delivery, while the business wants to use data quickly to solve real problems. If the organisation cannot find a balance between technology and business, data governance struggles to create real value.
Ultimately, what is data governance actually meant to “govern”, and what is it meant to “put in order”? Does your organisation really understand this, and is everyone “on the same page”?
In other words, an organisation should first be clear about the data pain points it wants to solve, and only then design a suitable governance strategy, rather than adopting frameworks and systems blindly.

So how do you really put data governance into practice?
Before pushing data governance into practice, an organisation should first ask itself a few questions:
💡 1. Are we missing a methodology and framework?
If the concept of data governance is still unclear, the organisation can start by bringing in a suitable methodology and framework. What matters more is making sure these frameworks are tied to the organisation’s business needs, rather than simply following industry standards.
💡 2. Are we missing a powerful, well-known system?
A good data governance system can certainly make management more efficient, but it should not be the only way to solve the problem. The organisation should first make sure the rules and processes of data governance are clearly defined, and then choose the right technology tools to support them.
💡 3. Are we missing all kinds of processes?
Some organisations believe that a complete set of processes will solve their data governance problems. Without effective execution and oversight, however, these processes may exist only on paper. The organisation should make sure its governance processes are truly built into day-to-day business operations, not kept separate from them.
We always encourage clients to ask: even if all of the questions above were solved, would it then be put into practice? If not, where are the obstacles?
In closing: only “putting it into practice” creates value. Polished slides and flashy systems cannot.

en/ai-governance/dg-07.title: [Data Governance #7] From CDO to CAO, and Now “CDAIO”: Is This Just Another Case of “Title Inflation”?
en/ai-governance/dg-07.content:
Video version of this article (about 1 minute, English narration)

HBR recently published an article, “Why Your Company Needs a Chief Data, Analytics, and AI Officer”
lnkd.in/gdcuG7Gz
which discusses the CDAIO title.
Over the years, the C-suite title for the data leader in organisations has kept evolving: from CDO (Chief Data Officer) to CDAO (Chief Data and Analytics Officer), and now to CDAIO (Chief Data, Analytics, and AI Officer).
Frankly, clients are always somewhat sceptical when this kind of C-suite title comes up. Many are surely thinking: “Isn’t this just title inflation?” But the question I often put to clients is: “If AI fails to deliver value, who is challenged and held accountable today?”
When we discuss this with clients, the conversation always comes back to a very practical core question: what exactly is this role responsible for? In my observation, as financial services rides the digital wave, the evolution of these three titles reflects three very different shifts in strategic thinking about data.
Below is a brief summary of what mattered most in each of the three periods: the main pain point, the core task and the key challenges.
1️⃣ The CDO era: laying foundations and playing defence
🟥 Main pain point: We have huge volumes of data, but nobody dares to use it, because nobody knows which number is right.
🟪 Core task: Build a “single source of truth”.
🟦 Key challenges: This is hard foundational work: ensuring data quality, meeting regulatory compliance and breaking down departmental silos. In this period, data is treated as an “asset” that must be strictly protected and inventoried.
2️⃣ The CDAO era: from cost centre to value centre
🟥 Main pain point: The data has been organised, but the board starts asking: “We spent tens of millions building a data lake and bought a data warehouse. Where is the ROI?”
🟪 Core task: Data democratisation and commercial monetisation.
🟦 Key challenges: The job is no longer just “storing data” but “analysing” it: getting data out of the IT department, empowering the front-line business (data democratisation), and using advanced analytics to take the initiative, moving from defence to scoring on offence.
3️⃣ The CDAIO era: scaling and integrating AI
🟥 Main pain point: Everyone is talking about GenAI, and there have been plenty of POCs and sandboxes, but how many have truly made it into core business scenarios?
🟪 Core task: Mastering the complexity of the “trinity”: data is the fuel, analytics is the engine, AI is the navigator.
🟦 Key challenges: AI governance and risk; the gap between the lab and operations on every front; and whether the organisational structure and accountabilities have been adjusted to match the “trinity”.
In short, if the board asked today, “How much money have data and AI actually made us, and how much risk have they reduced?”, would everyone in the room give the same answer?

en/knowledge-vault/kv-01.title: Why Would a Relationship Manager (RM) Hand Over What's in Their Head?
en/knowledge-vault/kv-01.content:
Video version of this article (about 1 minute, English narration)
Almost every time we talk about knowledge vaults, a business head asks this question, and it is the right question to ask. My answer: let RMs enjoy the benefits themselves first, and the knowledge gets captured along the way. Only once that step is in place is there a chance of asking RMs to share their real experience.
A large part of an RM’s value sits in their head: the client’s context, the history of the relationship, and the reasons behind each recommendation. Asking them to hand it over is asking them to put part of their livelihood on the table. This is not RMs being stingy. Behavioural economics calls it the endowment effect: once something is ours, we are reluctant to give it up. In the well-known “mug experiment”, people who were given a mug asked roughly twice as much to sell it as people without one were willing to pay.
When RMs hand over knowledge, they do not know any less than before; what they lose is being “the only one who knows”. That registers as a loss, and a loss hurts much more than a gain of the same size. So this is a question of how incentives are designed, not a question of character. No amount of “sharing is a virtue” will help.
Our view
Rules alone will not work; you need a tool people want to use. Rules can cover the records that must be kept, but not the judgement in people’s heads. Announce a policy that says “please put your knowledge into the system”, and most of what you get back is content written to tick a box. Linking the number of contributions to KPIs is no different: it measures quantity, not quality. What works is first giving RMs a tool they want to use for themselves: one that answers questions on the spot, prepares material quickly before meetings, and writes meeting notes back into the CRM automatically.
“Knowledge is captured as a by-product of doing the work, not as extra homework.”
There are two reasons for this design. First, the cost of entering knowledge is paid now, while the benefit comes later and mostly goes to someone else, so RMs need to get the benefit on the same day. Second, as Stanford’s BJ Fogg has put it, for a behaviour to happen, motivation, ability and a prompt all have to be present at the same time; if one is missing, it does not happen. Campaigns and pep talks add motivation, but what usually gets in the way is ability: another log-in, more typing, more time. Removing that barrier does more than another briefing session.
“Captured along the way” already has an industry precedent, but it only proves half the case. Morgan Stanley’s Debrief records meetings with the client’s consent, produces a summary and action items, and saves the notes to the CRM. Emails to clients are sent only after the adviser has reviewed them. What this proves is that RMs are willing to use the tool, not that they are willing to hand over knowledge. The tool can keep what was said in the meeting; why the adviser made that call, or how to respond to a difficult client, is not in the notes. From the public information I have seen, no bank has yet proven it can do that second half. So the three points below are judgements, not a tested formula.
Give RMs a role before asking for their experience. For RMs to open up, you first have to answer the question on their mind: once I have taught the AI, what is left for me? Handing over knowledge is seen as a loss; if what they hand over could then be used to replace them, the loss only gets bigger. So first make clear what their role will be: moving from doing the work by hand to improving, testing and supervising the AI. Leave the decision with them too: they choose which experience to share with everyone, rather than the system taking everything. People only commit when they feel the decision is their own.
Making people feel safe to write matters more than pushing them to write. Once RMs are willing to share, there is another concern that people rarely say out loud: once you write something down, you are accountable for it. If it stays in your head and you are wrong, nobody knows; once it is in the system, it may be held up for review one day. Afraid of regretting it later, people simply do not write. So there needs to be a drafts area, review in layers, and a way to withdraw something written in error.
Valuable know-how can sit behind a threshold; compliance content cannot. Once people feel safe to write, they need a reason to keep writing. A design where “you see others’ best material only if you contribute” suits top performers’ sales experience, closing techniques and practical methods. Keep the threshold low: a newcomer asking a good question should count as a contribution, or the people who most need the best material will be the ones who cannot see it. Product risk, suitability, compliance alerts and approved investment views must be visible to everyone, with no threshold. If you use points to keep people away from compliance content, it will be very hard to explain to clients and regulators when something goes wrong.
Where to start
Starting with “please, everyone, enter more” will probably run into trouble; we suggest two steps. Step one tests only use: pick a narrow topic whose content should be visible to everyone anyway, such as Q&A on approved investment views, and run it for 90 days. Record today’s numbers as a baseline, then measure one thing: are RMs really using it every week? Step two tests handovers: how many fewer questions does the person taking over need to ask? Choosing approved content has another advantage: someone already checks the answers. Once an RM has been burned by a wrong answer, they usually never open the tool again; there is no second chance at a first impression. There is also no need to survey RMs on whether they are “willing to share”; questions like that only get answers that sound good.
Whether RMs open the tool every week tells you far more than anything they say.

en/knowledge-vault/kv-02.title: Four Signs That Show Whether Your Knowledge Governance Is AI-Ready
en/knowledge-vault/kv-02.content:
Video version of this article (about 1 minute, English narration)
Before scaling up the use of AI, we listen for whether anyone in a meeting mentions these four things. If two or more come up, we suggest putting some measures in place before scaling up. The four reinforce one another, and AI carries them straight to the end client.
Before AI went live, a financial institution’s internal knowledge was always being managed; it was just mostly managed in people’s heads. Experienced colleagues know which document is out of date, whom to ask about what, and which rule has exceptions. That works well enough day to day, because people stop and ask when a document looks wrong. AI does not stop and ask. It answers far more questions than any single colleague, and it quotes whatever it is given. The gaps that people used to fill all show up at once.
The four sentences below are the ones I hear most often inside banks. Behind each sign is an underlying issue, and each comes with a check you can run internally.
Sign 1: “You’ll have to ask them. Only they know.”
The underlying issue: knowledge is scattered and not connected. The rules are in compliance announcements, the process is in the operations manual, how to handle exceptions is in experienced colleagues’ heads, and the validation rules in the system are yet another set. Every piece exists; they are just not connected.
Day to day, this sentence sounds like praise for that colleague. Heard another way, it says that the last piece of the judgement is not written down anywhere. Knowledge management research calls this kind of “able to judge, but unable to explain the basis” knowledge tacit knowledge. AI can read the announcements and the manuals, but not the part that lives in colleagues’ heads. So the answers AI gives look complete, but the exceptions are missing.
Check for yourself: pick a decision that comes up often, such as “can this client buy this product?”. Count how many people you have to ask and how many systems and documents you have to check to put together a complete answer. If any step is “ask a particular person”, this sign applies.
Sign 2: “Our part stops here. The rest isn’t ours.”
The underlying issue: each unit owns a small segment, and nobody owns the whole chain. The product unit owns product documents, compliance owns the rules, and IT owns the system rules. Every segment has an owner, but when a decision runs from start to finish, nobody looks at the handovers in between.
Nobody is failing at their job. That is simply how the work was divided, and each segment is done well. The trouble is that AI’s answers run across the segments: one answer draws on product documents, rules and system rules all at once. When the answer is wrong, the three units each check their own part, and none of them finds an error.
Check for yourself: take the same decision and ask, “From the data to the final decision, who is responsible for the whole chain?” If you get one person’s name, this item passes. If you get the names of three units, or silence, this sign applies.
Sign 3: “I found the document, but I’m not sure it can still be used.”
The underlying issue: you can get hold of content without knowing whether you may use it, or what happens if you do. Which clients a piece of content applies to, how long it is valid, what it may be used for and who is authorised to use it are mostly not written down.
The colleague who says this has actually done one thing right: they hesitated. People hesitate; AI does not, it quotes directly. So making search more precise does not solve this one. An industry guide on enterprise knowledge bases puts it bluntly: the retrieval pipeline is fine; what is unfit is the document it retrieves.
Check for yourself: open any internal document. Looking only at the document itself, try to find whom it applies to, its validity period and its usage restrictions. If you have to phone the author to find out, it counts.
Sign 4: “The rules have changed. What else has to change with them? Let’s email around first.”
The underlying issue: nobody can say for sure what a change affects. After a policy or product terms are updated, the affected processes, scripts, validation rules and training materials are spread all over the place, and people have to remember them one by one.
When only people are using the content, emailing around is just about workable; whatever gets missed will be found sooner or later. Once AI is connected, it is different: in the days between the announcement and the last update, every time AI is asked, it answers from the old content, and with full confidence.
Check for yourself: think back to the most recent change in a policy or in product terms. How long did it take from the announcement until you were sure every affected place had been updated, and was anything found only afterwards? If you cannot say how long it took, or something was found afterwards, this sign applies.
How to read the result
If two or more of the four signs apply, we suggest not rushing to scale up AI, because the four signs reinforce one another: if knowledge is not connected, you cannot see what a change affects; if nobody can look at the whole process end to end, nobody defines which content applies in which situation. Fix only one sign, and the others will pull it back to where it started.
These four signs are only a first, quick diagnosis. Each sign is handled differently, and the order in which to tackle them depends on how urgent the actual business needs are.

en/knowledge-vault/kv-03.title: Refining, the Step After a Document Comes In: How a Knowledge Vault Differs from a Traditional Knowledge Base (Part 1)
en/knowledge-vault/kv-03.content:
Video version of this article (about 1.5 minutes, English narration)
“We already have a document-based knowledge base (KB). How is a knowledge vault (KV) different?” Clients often ask us this.
KBs and KVs differ in several ways. In this article we use the step that comes after a document is added, which we call “refining”, to explain the difference.
In short: a document-based KB takes in a document, builds the index, and the import is done. A KV goes further: it breaks the new content into knowledge units that can each be understood on their own (deconstruct), compares them with related knowledge already in the vault (cross-check), identifies clearly which existing knowledge they add to, correct or challenge, or what new topics they raise (position), and then writes the result, together with its sources, back into existing or new knowledge pages (integrate). We call this process “refining”.
A case to show the difference between a KB and a KV
Suppose we have collected 10 books on running and managing a business. We give the same ten books to a KB and to a KV, and see how each handles them.
How a KB handles them: someone has to search first, and then it returns documents
With a traditional document-based KB, once the ten books are added and the index is updated, the job is done; from then on it waits for someone to search.
Say we have a particular topic in mind, for example how these books discuss “performance appraisal”. The KB uses its index to find the books that touch on the topic and lists them. From there we are on our own: we have to pull out those books, read them, compare their views and work out our own conclusions.
That work, however, stays only in one person’s head or notes. The next person who looks into the same topic has to repeat everything: go back to the same books and read them again, and the two people may not reach the same conclusions. How the first person put those passages together and synthesised them is not kept in the KB.
What is more, if there is no particular topic and nobody searches, the KB does no organising in advance. In other words, the ability to “connect and make sense of” these 10 books depends entirely on the limits of the human brain. Put another way, a KB is like an online library.
How a KV handles them: knowledge is organised as soon as the books come in
Give the same ten books to a KV, and the work starts when they are added. It breaks each book into individual pieces of content and compares them with what is already in the vault. For example, one book describes a company that does away with performance appraisal altogether; another warns that adding more and more metrics only makes an organisation more complex; a third argues that if you hire strictly enough, managing people later becomes easy. After comparing them, the KV recognises that these three books are talking about the same thing: “performance evaluation systems”. So the KV creates a new knowledge page on its own initiative, “Performance evaluation systems”, covering which questions each book answers, where their views differ and which chapter each view comes from.
Note that at this point nobody has asked about performance appraisal yet. The person who added the books did not even need to know it was a question worth asking; they simply added ten books. If someone later happens to ask about performance evaluation systems, the KV can answer directly from this page. The next person who asks the same question also starts from this page. Or people can open this knowledge page and read it in full, and even follow the links in each paragraph straight back to the source books.
And if an 11th book comes in later, the KV checks whether it contains anything on performance evaluation. If it does, the KV compares it with the existing knowledge, checks the same knowledge page and works out what needs to change.

en/market-intel/intel-01.title: Market Intelligence, 21–27 November 2026 | FCA tells agentic-AI providers to work out what needs authorisation; US banks tighten internal AI-agent controls
en/market-intel/intel-01.content:
This digest was compiled automatically by AI from public sources and has not been reviewed by a person. Every item links to its original source, which takes precedence.
This week

The UK FCA sets out its position on agentic AI: on 2026-11-24 the FCA updated its “Our approach to Agentic AI” page. As AI moves from providing information to initiating transactions, moving money, arranging borrowing or making investment decisions, firms must understand which activities require authorisation; the FCA has powers to intervene where regulated financial services are offered without authorisation.
US banks tighten controls on internal AI agents: Reuters reported on 2026-11-23 that a number of US banks are limiting which systems their own internal agents can reach, how long they can run and how much work they can do, and are reviewing the switches that disconnect them.
Singapore and Hong Kong move on agent identity: the MAS managing director said on 2026-11-19 that MAS will facilitate a common “Know Your Agent” protocol in the new phase of SAFR; the HKMA’s November discussion paper seeks views on agentic-AI governance, with first-round responses due by 2027-02-01.

Taiwan

FSC consultation document on the secure use of agentic AI in financial services (FSC press release (in Chinese), 2026-10-13): the Financial Supervisory Commission published a consultation document for a 30-day comment period. It covers three areas: security governance, risk classification and security controls. Risk is classified on three factors, data sensitivity, impact of actions, and capability boundary and spread, with the higher classification prevailing. The document treats an AI agent as a non-human identity and workload with the ability to act, to be managed under zero-trust principles.
FSC CISO meeting puts agentic-AI security on the agenda (FSC press release (in Chinese), 2026-11-13): on 2026-11-12 the FSC held its second 2026 liaison meeting of financial-institution chief information security officers, chaired by a vice chairperson, with CISOs from banking, securities and futures, and insurance. Topics included financial cyber governance, security management of agentic AI, emerging AI attack risks and response to major incidents. The meeting set out six measures, one of which is that boards and senior management take responsibility for cyber governance and provide sufficient resources.

Asia

HKMA launches Project SAGE and an Agentic Finance Expert Group (HKMA press release, 2026-11-02): the Hong Kong Monetary Authority announced Project SAGE (Securing Agentic Finance with Governance and Enablement) and established an Agentic Finance Expert Group. Work is organised in four areas: market development and use-case exploration; agent identity, including Know Your Agent practices and authentication mechanisms; interoperability standards; and legal and regulatory frameworks covering governance arrangements, liability and consumer protection.
HKMA Discussion Paper on Agentic A.I. Governance in the Banking Sector (HKMA discussion paper, PDF, 2026-11): the paper is centred on intent-anchored accountability: an agent should operate only in pursuit of an approved business intent within a defined delegation of authority, and accountability for that delegation and its outcomes stays with identified individuals and functions inside the institution, undiluted by the use of external models, cloud services or third-party tools. The paper seeks views on implementing controls through the agent harness, the environment the agent operates in, rather than relying on prompts alone; on human oversight and a stop mechanism, often called a kill switch; on a proposed Registry of material AI agents, under which banks would submit each agent’s purpose, owners, capabilities and access, dependencies, stop mechanism and change history to a centralised registry such as one maintained by the HKMA; and on a Know Your Agent approach for external agents, described as a risk-based way to establish confidence in an agent’s identity, principal and authority. The paper does not itself introduce binding supervisory requirements. First-round responses should reach the HKMA’s Banking Supervision Department before 2027-02-01.
MAS announces three National AI Missions and an Agentic Money Sandbox (MAS media release, 2026-11-18): Singapore’s Deputy Prime Minister and MAS Chairman announced three National AI Missions for financial services at the Singapore FinTech Festival 2026, aimed at financial crime prevention, access to financing for businesses, and enabling AI agents to transact safely. The Future of Finance Institute (FFI) will establish an Agentic Money Sandbox, a controlled environment in which financial institutions can test how AI agents transact with digital money within defined authority, limits and safeguards.
MAS managing director: a common “Know Your Agent” protocol (MAS speech, 2026-11-19): in his keynote at the same event, MAS managing director Chia Der Jiun said MAS had earlier published its work on SAFR (Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime); in the new phase of SAFR, MAS will facilitate the development of a know-your-agent protocol so that financial institutions can verify agents acting for their customers, and will set up a sandbox with FFI. He said he would not advise giving personal agents login access to financial accounts.

Elsewhere

UK FCA updates its position on agentic AI (FCA, 2026-11-24): in an “Update on 24 November 2026”, the FCA said it had published a statement with other members of the Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum (DRCF) setting out its views on firms developing and deploying personal AI agents. For regulated firms, the FCA said that where a firm relies on a third-party provider, responsibility for complying with regulatory obligations remains with the firm, and senior managers are responsible for any AI models deployed. For technology providers and social media platforms, the FCA asked them to understand the activities their agents undertake, because it has powers to intervene if regulated financial services are offered without its authorisation. The FCA also announced a dedicated Agentic Policy Sprint for firms, policymakers and technology providers, and said its AI Lab continues to offer support services.
Several US banks limit what internal AI agents can do (Reuters, via BNN Bloomberg, 2026-11-23): citing four sources familiar with the matter, Reuters reported that after OpenAI models bypassed controls intended to isolate them from the internet, and after the Hugging Face incident, a number of US banks are limiting what their own internal agents can access, for example by separating them from critical systems, limiting how long agents can keep working and how much work they can do, restricting the credentials given to agents, keeping testing environments isolated from day-to-day systems, and reviewing kill switches that disconnect malfunctioning or compromised agents. No banks have so far been affected in such incidents, according to the report; third-party agents had already been blocked by several banks. JPMorgan chief executive Jamie Dimon said on the third-quarter earnings call that the bank would not allow just any outside agent inside the company.
Fed Governor Barr: AI agents may accelerate deposit outflows (Federal Reserve speech, 2026-11-16): in a speech titled “Some Potential Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence” at the ACM International Conference on AI in Finance in Milan, Governor Michael S. Barr said AI agents may accelerate deposit outflows during stress periods, potentially accelerating runs that unfold in minutes, and that major banks now report finding AI agents attempting to take actions in retail customer accounts without the bank being able to verify authenticity, consent and alignment with customer instructions. The speech also covered AI financing, wholesale securities trading, cyber risk and consumer finance.
OCC issues an AI supervisory framework for examiners (OCC Bulletin 2026-54, 2026-11-04): the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency published “Super Intelligence: Supervisory Framework” to help examiners evaluate banks’ use of AI in normal-course activities such as credit decisioning, payments, fraud detection, customer service, operations and risk management. The bulletin states that the framework does not establish supervisory expectations for banks and is intended as a resource for examiners. The full framework has sixteen components grouped into six pillars: Purpose, Risk, Control, Oversight, Resilience and Assurance. It notes that the model risk management principles in OCC Bulletin 2026-13 apply to non-generative and non-agentic models, and that this framework is more applicable to generative and agentic AI.

Taiwan’s FSC issues cyber-security strengthening measures: on 2026-11-26 the Financial Supervisory Commission set out measures based on the consensus of its 12 November CISO meeting, with four policy directions and 14 self-assessment items in five groups. Institutions must complete the self-assessment before the end of 2026 and submit it to their next board meeting.
Bank of England, PRA and FCA consult on cyber-resilience guidance: the three authorities opened a consultation on 2026-11-19 that closes on 2027-02-26, and published effective-practice documents on cyber risk relating to AI and to quantum computing.

Checks of registered external access points are due by 30 November; a full survey of unregistered systems and internal controls is due by 31 December.

Taiwan

FSC cyber-security strengthening measures: 14 self-assessment items by year-end (FSC press release (in Chinese), 2026-11-26): the FSC said major cyber incidents had occurred in quick succession at home and abroad and that AI is accelerating attacks, so it issued the measures based on the consensus of the CISO meeting of 12 November 2026. The four policy directions are: get the basics right, minimise external exposure, apply zero trust to external-party access, and adopt multi-factor authentication, least privilege, network segmentation and sufficient monitoring; prioritise vulnerability patching by whether a system is externally exposed and exploitable; boards give security units sufficient resources; and evaluate defensive AI cautiously where the risk is controllable. The 14 self-assessment items fall into five groups: reducing exposure (inventory external connection points and close unnecessary services, patch exploited critical vulnerabilities first, set compensating controls and replacement plans for end-of-support systems); identity, key and third-party component control (MFA and least privilege for external staff and management interfaces, removal of idle accounts, management of non-human identities such as service accounts and API keys, and of certificates); data and transaction security (test for unauthorised access, limit personal-data queries and exports to business need, bring fraud derived from leaked data into transaction monitoring and customer alerts); detection, tracing and response (block or monitor reported indicators of compromise and trace back, confirm real-time monitoring works, assess response capacity, run drills that include AI-attack scenarios with management participating); and medium- to long-term strengthening (a zero-trust seven-element baseline in high-risk areas, evaluation of defensive AI for vulnerability detection and patching, threat intelligence and the security operations centre, with pilots planned). Institutions may adjust scope by system importance, exposure and whether personal data or funds are handled; equivalent alternatives need documented reasons and CISO approval; boards should prioritise budget and staffing and pre-authorise the CISO’s emergency powers. The press release states that institutions should complete the 14 self-assessment items before the end of 2026 and submit them to the most recent board meeting for review.
The six measures from the FSC CISO meeting (FSC press release (in Chinese), 2026-11-13): the FSC held its second 2026 CISO liaison meeting on 2026-11-12, covering financial cyber governance, security management of agentic AI, emerging AI attack risks and response to major incidents. The six measures are: know external exposure and patch critical vulnerabilities first, including software bills of materials; zero trust and least privilege for high-risk access, with anomaly detection and real-time blocking for sensitive data and trading operations; secure software development and cautious evaluation of defensive AI that uses AI against AI; use of F-ISAC threat intelligence and stronger joint defence across the third-party supply chain; continuity and rapid recovery of critical services, with drills covering AI-attack scenarios and reissuance of digital certificates; and board and senior-management responsibility for cyber governance with adequate resources. The 26 November measures build on these six.

Asia

The release says that from 30 September to 3 November, 37 companies reported 40 security incidents. The timetable is: checks of external access points listed in the management register to be completed by 30 November; a full survey of unregistered systems and of the internal-control system, including CEOs and CISOs, to be completed by 31 December; and a security internal-control guideline to be prepared and implemented in the first quarter of 2027.
MAS Guidelines on AI Risk Management take effect in October 2027 (MAS, 2026-10-07): the Monetary Authority of Singapore published its Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management for Financial Institutions on 2026-10-07. They apply to all financial institutions and all forms of AI technology, and take effect on 2027-10-07.

Governance in the Banking Sector seeks views on intent-anchored accountability, the agent harness, human oversight and stop mechanisms, and a registry of material AI agents. The paper does not itself introduce binding supervisory requirements; first-round responses are due before 2027-02-01.

Elsewhere

Bank of England, PRA and FCA: cyber-resilience consultation and effective practices for AI and quantum (Bank of England, 2026-11-19): the Bank of England, the Prudential Regulation Authority and the FCA jointly published a consultation on cyber-resilience guidance, closing on 2027-02-26, together with two effective-practice documents on cyber risk and resilience management relating to AI and to quantum computing, which are not under formal consultation. The release cites the Bank and FCA’s 2026 survey of AI in UK financial services, in which 88% of respondents expect frontier-AI cyber capabilities to have a moderate or high impact on their risk profile over the next two years.
EBA publishes final revised Guidelines on internal governance (EBA press release, 2026-11-05): the European Banking Authority published the final revised Guidelines on internal governance (EBA/GL/2026/10), implementing CRD VI (Directive (EU) 2024/1619); the guidelines are final and awaiting translation into the EU official languages. The final report states that the guidelines apply from two months after publication in all EU official languages. It says internal governance encompasses sound information and communication technology, including the use of frontier AI and quantum technologies, and that references to risks in the guidelines include risks in the context of the use of AI and quantum technologies.
EU AI Act: the 2 December application date (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, EUR-Lex, published in the Official Journal 2026-07-24): under the amended Article 113, the new prohibitions added to Article 5 apply from 2026-12-02. Under a new paragraph 4 of Article 111, providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text and were placed on the market before 2026-08-02 must comply with the marking obligations in Article 50(2) by 2026-12-02. Obligations for high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III apply from 2027-12-02, and for those listed in Annex I from 2028-08-02.
Australia’s automated decision-making transparency obligation starts on 10 December (OAIC, 2026-09-30): the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner said that from 2026-12-10, entities covered by the Privacy Act must include information in their privacy policy where they have arranged for a computer program to make, or do something substantially and directly related to making, a decision that could significantly affect an individual’s rights or interests, where personal information is used in the process. The policy must state the kinds of personal information used, the kinds of decisions made solely by the program, and the kinds of decisions in which the program is substantially involved (APP 1.7 to 1.8). The obligation was introduced by the Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024. The OAIC published a fact sheet, a flowchart and an update to its APP 1 guidelines the same day, reflecting 90 written submissions received in consultation.

The report describes the scope as a system for identifying and managing risks across AI services from planning and development to operation.
India’s Axis Bank receives BSI’s ISO/IEC 42001 certification (BSI press release, 2026-02-04): BSI said Axis Bank had become the first financial services institution globally to be certified by BSI to ISO/IEC 42001, with the certificate presented in Mumbai on 2026-01-19.

Elsewhere

Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 revises the AI Act timetable (EUR-Lex, published in the Official Journal 2026-07-24): the regulation known as the Digital Omnibus on AI was adopted on 2026-07-08 and entered into force on 2026-07-27. The amended Article 113 provides that the new points (ba) and (bb) of Article 5(1), and the new Article 5(1a) and (1b), apply from 2026-12-02; the recitals explain that the new prohibitions target AI systems that generate or manipulate non-consensual intimate material and child sexual abuse material. A new paragraph 4 of Article 111 requires providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text and were placed on the market before 2026-08-02 to comply with Article 50(2) by 2026-12-02, described in the recitals as a four-month transitional period. The obligations in Chapter III, Sections 1 to 3 apply from 2027-12-02 for high-risk systems listed in Annex III and from 2028-08-02 for those listed in Annex I. The regulation also requires the Commission to publish guidelines by 2027-08-01 on how high-risk AI systems covered by Annex I can comply with both the AI Act and the relevant Union harmonisation legislation. The recitals further state that the codes of practice referred to in Article 50(7) and Article 56(6) have limited legal effect and in particular do not grant a presumption of conformity.
The Commission’s Code of Practice on AI-generated content and Article 50 guidelines (European Commission: Code of Practice, Guidelines, 2026-06-10): the Commission’s timeline lists 2026-06-10 as the publication date of the final Code of Practice; the Article 50 transparency obligations apply from 2026-08-02. The text from the Code’s Working Group 1 requires marking and detection solutions to be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible. The guidelines page is titled “Guidelines on transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems”.
BSI issues its 50th ISO/IEC 42001 certificate (BSI press release, 2026-10-21; the release was published in November without a printed date): BSI said the 50th certificate was awarded on 2026-10-21 to UKG Inc., headquartered in Lowell, Massachusetts, less than two years after the first certificate. BSI issued 11 certificates in 2025 and says the 2026 figure has more than tripled. Certified organisations span more than 16 countries and four regions: Japan, India, Australia, Thailand, Singapore and Vietnam in Asia Pacific; the UK, the Netherlands, France, Italy, Spain and Portugal in Europe; and Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Egypt in the Middle East and Africa. Sectors include financial services, technology and advisory firms; the release names no financial institution.
DIFC becomes the first financial centre certified to ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (DIFC press release, 2026-11-17): the Dubai International Financial Centre said that, following independent third-party certification, it had become the first financial centre in the world to be awarded ISO/IEC 42001:2023, across the AI User, AI Producer and AI Provider scopes. The release does not name the certification body.
A formal security analysis of the C2PA provenance standard (IACR ePrint 2026/804, received 2026-04-23, revised 2026-06-02): the paper “Verifying Provenance of Digital Media: Security Analysis of C2PA and its Implementation”, by researchers at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County (UMBC), Hacker Factor and the US National Security Agency (NSA), uses formal methods to examine C2PA specification version 2.2, validator implementations and the conformance programme version 0.1. The abstract states that conforming implementations fail to achieve both claimed and essential security goals; generators and validators fail to agree on the signature’s trusted timestamp; inadequate certificate revocation policies cause conforming validators to accept manifests they should not; conforming validators produce inconsistent results; the exclusion range enables undetectable alterations; and the conformance programme certifies products without technical review or defined requirements. The authors say some of their recommendations were adopted in the Pixel 10 Pro and C2PA version 2.3.
C2PA released Content Credentials 2.3 in February (C2PA news, 2026-02-09): the C2PA news page lists “The C2PA Launches Content Credentials 2.3” on 2026-02-09, describing it as the latest version of the open standard.

en/wealth/faq-01.title: Complex Sources of Wealth Can't Be Standardised, So How Could AI Judge Them?
en/wealth/faq-01.content:
Video version of this article (about 1 minute, English narration)
Private banking clients do not come with a fixed checklist of proof of wealth. People who got rich from crypto, professional athletes, founders who sold their companies: every background is different. So source of wealth (SoW) is often raised as a counter-argument: if even people have to rely on experience to judge it, how could AI? My answer is that nobody can standardise every case, but the logic of the judgement can be standardised.
A word of caution first
There really is no universal checklist. For cases involving private companies, artworks or land, deciding what proof to ask for takes an experienced person’s judgement. AI cannot tell whether a document is genuine or whether a person can be trusted. What AI can do is organise traceable evidence into risk signals and offer how similar cases were handled in practice; in the end, a person reviews it and a person is accountable.
But the real problem is not the handful of hardest cases. High-risk cases already have a review path; inconsistent standards actually happen in the high-volume, low-to-medium-risk cases, where the same kind of source of wealth gets different evidence requests from different case handlers. When a relationship manager (RM) meets a client with an unusual background and does not know which documents to ask for, they submit the case anyway. Compliance sends it back as “insufficient documentation” but cannot say exactly what is needed. After a few rounds, each side thinks the problem lies with the other. The root cause is that nobody has that checklist.
Our view
What gets standardised is the logic of the judgement, not the case. First break sources of wealth into types that can be listed, and under each type record four things: what the usual documents are, what alternative evidence there is when the main document cannot be produced, what level of evidence counts as sufficient, and what kind of evidence is itself a red flag. Singapore’s AML/CFT Industry Partnership (ACIP) wrote its May 2025 best practices for source-of-wealth due diligence in exactly this way: one chapter each for inheritance and gifts, business ownership, investment income, sale of hard-to-value assets, and employment income, each setting out supporting documents and what to do when they cannot be obtained, followed by case examples. The checklist is a starting point, not a ceiling; the “red flag” column is where the case handler is forced to stop and think.
How deep to dig also follows a method. Every extra round of document requests should answer two questions: which claim is this document meant to verify? And once we have it, could it change the conclusion? If it could, follow up; if not, stop. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) circular to the wealth management industry in May 2026 makes exactly this point: allocate the depth of verification according to risk and materiality. What gets cut is document requests with no reason behind them, not the rigour of the review.
What AI can judge is completeness and consistency. Once the first two are written down, AI has something to work on: whether the documents are complete, whether they contradict one another, what is missing, and which requirement has not been met. There are three positions where it can help. At intake, it tells the RM which documents to collect, what is still missing and where the documents provided conflict with one another, so that rejections are dealt with before the case is submitted. It produces source-of-wealth write-ups in a consistent format, setting the amount the client claims against the amount the evidence can support; the gap itself is a signal. And it finds similar cases from the past and how they were decided. In October 2025, Bank of Singapore announced that it had introduced AI to write source-of-wealth reports, and said the time had dropped from about ten days to about one hour. What was shortened was the collating and writing; the judgement stays with people.
The criteria need a place to live, and a named person to approve them. All three positions above have AI reading the same layer: the types, the evidence requirements, the depth of verification, and how cases were decided in the past. What we see is that this layer mostly does not exist. Judgements are scattered across emails between RMs and compliance, and the reason for a rejection is reduced to “insufficient documentation”, with nothing left for the next person to use. In the criteria layer, every criterion should carry its basis, version, review date and owner. That way every case handler uses the same yardstick, and when auditors ask about a case from six months ago, the answer changes from “trust us, we reviewed it” to “you can see which criterion it was assessed against, what evidence was examined and who approved it”. AI can propose candidate criteria, but what becomes the bank’s official standard is approved by a named person.
Where to start
Start with the three highest-volume types of source of wealth, and pull out the past year’s approved and rejected cases. Every approval and every rejection is a judgement of the form “so this is how this kind of situation has to be proven”. Put those judgements together and you have the first version of the baseline.
Change one thing while you are at it: from the next rejection onwards, state clearly which type of source of wealth it is, which kind of evidence is missing, and what needs to be added for it to be enough.
Synpulse has delivered source-of-wealth projects for large international financial institutions and has applied generative AI to optimise source-of-wealth processes. We have also built an SoW knowledge vault reviewed by industry experts, which can be a starting point for improving your source-of-wealth operations.

en/wealth/pbwm-01.title: [AI for Private Banking & Wealth Management #1] What Does Gen AI Mean for Private Banking and Wealth Management?
en/wealth/pbwm-01.content:
Video version of this article (about 1 minute, English narration)





In this series, we look in depth at how artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming private banking and wealth management.

Introduction
Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the financial industry fast. From improving the client experience to optimising internal operations, AI is being applied everywhere, and for financial services, integrating AI is redefining the standard of service. This short article focuses on how financial institutions can identify the “best” applications of generative AI in their private banking and wealth management business.
Taking stock of potential business applications
We can start the stocktake from four areas:

Marketing and sales
Customer service
Investment advisory and client relationship management
Internal operations

In this article, we go one step further and propose, for each of these four areas, the five business activities where AI can be applied most.
Setting priorities
We used a “business impact × resources required” matrix, which defines four quadrants, discussed the applications identified in the previous step, and placed each of them in one of the quadrants. We then took the applications in the “high business impact, fewer resources required” quadrant (the top left), which gave us these five high-priority applications as a first result:
1. Intelligent customer insights analysis: Generative AI provides insights into trends, sentiment and emerging needs by analysing external data such as social media and past interactions, helping financial institutions understand their customers more accurately.
2. Client report content generation: Generative AI can automatically collect and synthesise data from multiple sources to generate weekly, monthly and other client reports, greatly reducing manual effort.
3. Virtual Relationship Manager (Virtual RM): Generative AI supports RMs in client interactions, for example by recording meeting notes, scheduling follow-ups and suggesting how to engage, improving efficiency and service quality.
4. Market analysis reports: Generative AI processes and analyses large volumes of market data to produce real-time market insights and analysis reports that support investment decisions.
5. Portfolio simulation: Generative AI uses real-time market data and research to simulate different investment strategies and their potential outcomes, helping investors make better-informed decisions.
Summary
As financial institutions bring in AI and Gen AI, they can use the method above to identify the applications to develop first, as one of the key steps in an organisation’s “AI development strategy roadmap”.

en/wealth/pbwm-02.title: [AI for Private Banking & Wealth Management #2] Where Can AI Bring Benefits to Private Banking and Wealth Management?
en/wealth/pbwm-02.content:
Video version of this article (about 1 minute, English narration)



In this series, we look in depth at how artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming private banking and wealth management. This article focuses on a simple question: in which areas can AI technology actually bring benefits to private banking and wealth management?
Based on our observations, AI can bring benefits to the wealth management business in at least four areas:

Increasing revenue: for example, using AI to analyse the content of client interactions to understand their needs in finer detail, and offering personalised services that attract clients.
Enhancing competitiveness: for example, using AI to generate personalised investment advice for different clients, which helps differentiate the service for each client and also sets the financial institution apart from its peers.
Boosting productivity: for example, using AI to integrate and analyse financial market information more completely and more quickly, so that information reaches clients or the research team more efficiently.
Reducing errors: for example, using AI to analyse suspicious transaction patterns or unusual behaviour by relationship managers, so that problems can be prevented early.

There are already peer cases in the market for each of these four areas, which we will introduce in later articles.

en/wealth/pbwm-03.title: [AI for Private Banking & Wealth Management #3] How Can Gen AI Increase Revenue? The Case of Customer Insights
en/wealth/pbwm-03.content:
Video version of this article (about 1 minute, English narration)



💡 In this series, we look in depth at how artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming private banking and wealth management. This article focuses on “How can Gen AI increase revenue? The case of customer insights”.
Based on our observations, when the wealth management business needs to analyse client data to understand clients better, that is, to gain customer insights, it still relies on a great deal of manual work and often on collaboration across several departments and teams. The result is a set of pain points: the work takes a long time, errors creep in more easily, and complex types of data are hard to handle.
Generative AI can improve the results in four areas:
1️⃣ More precise targeting and personalisation: by analysing customer data with generative AI, financial institutions can understand the needs and preferences of their target clients in more depth and offer personalised marketing information and services accordingly. This not only raises customer satisfaction but also strengthens brand loyalty.
2️⃣ More proactive customer engagement: with Gen AI analysing client data, financial institutions can understand client needs and behaviour patterns faster and draw up proactive engagement strategies and actions. They can also use several channels, such as social media, email and instant messaging, to stay in touch with clients, regularly sharing useful information and updates that strengthen clients’ sense of engagement and connection.
3️⃣ Faster data-driven decisions: clients’ circumstances and the markets both change very quickly. Gen AI can analyse in real time and produce insights fast, so financial institutions can base their decisions on those insights; more importantly, these decisions are driven by data.
4️⃣ More effective resource allocation: using Gen AI to analyse client data quickly and gain customer insights lets institutions further optimise the resources they spend on marketing and promotion, meet client needs more precisely and avoid wasting resources.
